strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap: existing visual grounding benchmarks focus on clean environments, missing real-world robustness challenges critical for safety-critical applications like autonomous driving

Large-scale, comprehensive benchmark with 38,760 instances featuring spatially aligned RGB-TIR pairs, rigorous filtering across three sources, and multi-level fine-grained annotations (13 scene types, 4 illumination conditions, 4 weather types, object sizes, occlusion)

Substantially more challenging dataset than predecessors: 23.1% weak-light samples (vs ~10% in RefCOCOg), 57.7% small objects (vs 45.4%), 14.24-word average queries (vs 8.47), with off-center object distributions reflecting real-world complexity

Unified RGBT-VG framework provides standardized infrastructure for fair comparison of multiple methods across RGB-only, TIR-only, and RGB-TIR settings, enabling systematic study of cross-modal effects

Extensive experimental evaluation across 60+ configurations with fine-grained analysis by scene type, weather, illumination, size, and occlusion; clear trends demonstrating RGB-TIR fusion benefits especially in challenging conditions
Comprehensive supplementary evaluation with 25+ fine-grained subsets showing stable method rankings across datasets, validating benchmark reliability

Well-designed baseline combining Asymmetric Modality Adaptation (recognizing TIR-specific adaptation needs) and Language-Aware Visual Synergy (using text to guide cross-modal fusion) with ablations demonstrating component effectiveness
Strong empirical results across benchmarks with RGBT-VGNet achieving best or second-best performance across most settings; promise to release all resources supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Critical annotation quality concerns: heavy reliance on LVLM (Qwen-VL) for automated annotation with no reported verification percentage, inter-annotator agreement scores, or Kappa metrics; this is problematic for a dataset paper where annotation quality directly impacts scientific conclusions

Insufficient transparency on annotation verification: mentions 'hierarchical random sampling' but provides no details on scale; statistical validation (Table 3) only checks physical plausibility of light-weather distributions, not accuracy of individual expressions or risk of LVLM hallucinations

Limited analysis of thermal imaging properties: claims thermal is 'illumination-invariant' but ignores emissivity variations, reflections, atmospheric effects, and sensor limitations; no TIR-specific failure mode analysis beyond low-light scenarios
Incomplete experimental results: missing entries in Tables 4-5 (D-MDETR and MMCA on RefM3FD marked with '-') with no explanation; impairs comparison fairness and completeness
No cross-dataset generalization evaluation (e.g., train on RefFLIR, test on RefM3FD) to assess whether learned patterns generalize across thermal sensor variations and environmental shifts

Limited evaluation metrics: only Acc@0.5 reported; Acc@0.75 would assess localization precision, while Acc@0.3 might be relevant for safety-critical applications; no analysis of performance sensitivity to resolution (fixed at 224×224 despite small-object focus)

Missing computational analysis: no inference time, memory, or computational cost comparison; no explicit per-modality contribution analysis despite claims of complementary strengths; no gradient-based or saliency analysis showing which modality drives predictions

Data source bias not addressed: datasets span different years (FLIR 2020, M3FD 2022, MFAD 2025) with potential domain shift; no discussion of geographic, demographic, or equipment-based biases inherited from source datasets or their representativeness for specific applications

Baseline novelty is limited though acceptable for benchmark paper: AMA is essentially asymmetric LoRA with different ranks (straightforward, lacking deeper insight); LAVS is standard text-guided cross-attention; modest absolute performance on hard cases (49.76% on small objects in RefMFAD)

Reproducibility gaps: exact Qwen-VL version and API parameters not specified; filtering rule implementation details unclear (e.g., exact thresholds); learning rate notation unusual (10e4); no convergence plots for 120-epoch training suggesting sufficient convergence

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real gaps in existing VG benchmarks: lack of environmental diversity, nighttime/low-light scenarios, and small/occluded objects
Comprehensive multi-level annotation scheme with fine-grained scene, environmental, and object-level labels enabling detailed analysis
Extensive empirical evaluation across 60+ configurations with multiple baselines and three sub-datasets revealing multi-modal vs uni-modal trade-offs
Unified RGBT-VG framework providing standardized implementation for adapting RGB methods to multi-modal settings
Detailed experimental results including ablation studies and qualitative visualizations demonstrating method effectiveness
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: RGBT-VGNet uses standard components (frozen CLIP + LoRA + cross-attention) with incremental contributions (asymmetric LoRA lacks principled justification; LAVS is standard attention)

Critical annotation quality concerns: relies on Qwen-VL black-box API with only informal human verification; no inter-annotator agreement metrics reported; no information on number of annotators or expertise level

Problematic dataset construction: filters out small objects (exactly where thermal helps most), reduces diversity by selecting largest instance per category, final size (38K instances) moderate relative to existing benchmarks (50-276K)

Insufficient validation: very small val sets (RefM³FD only 168 instances), no cross-dataset evaluation, no backward compatibility testing on RGB benchmarks, no statistical significance testing of improvements (often 1-3% gains)

Shallow analysis of multi-modal benefits: demonstrates multi-modal works better but lacks insight into why; no feature complementarity analysis; missing analysis of when thermal helps vs hurts; qualitative results are subjective cherry-picked examples

Limited ablation studies: only ablates AMA and LAVS; no ablations on LoRA ranks, attention variants, frozen vs fine-tuned encoders, fusion strategies; LAVS-only ablation missing with explanation suggesting problematic design coupling
Reproducibility concerns: code/data only promised in conclusion, depends on Qwen-VL API subject to future changes, specific hyperparameters missing, source dataset licensing/privacy not discussed
No comparison with alternative multi-modal fusion strategies or state-of-the-art RGB-Thermal methods from detection/segmentation literature; MV-* baselines are simple extensions not representing SOTA

strengths: Addresses genuine gap: First large-scale RGB-Thermal visual grounding benchmark for complex real-world scenarios with clear motivation for safety-critical applications

Comprehensive benchmark design: 40K images with multi-level annotations (13 scene types, 4 lighting/weather conditions), significantly higher proportions of challenging samples (57.7% small objects, 23.1% low-light), and longer queries (14.24 words)

Rigorous data construction pipeline: Careful three-stage filtering (visibility/scale, cross-modality alignment, category balance), LVLM-based annotation with human verification, and statistical validation of annotation quality
Unified RGBT-VG framework: Enables fair comparison by systematizing training, preprocessing, and evaluation across RGB-only, TIR-only, and RGB+TIR baselines on seven representative methods

Thorough experimental evaluation: 60+ configurations, specialized test splits (TestA/B/C), extensive fine-grained analysis across 25+ subsets (scenes, weather, illumination, sizes, occlusion), consistent method rankings across datasets, and effective ablations demonstrating component contributions

Strong empirical results: RGBT-VGNet achieves superior performance in challenging scenarios (nighttime: 67.19% vs 66.09%, small objects: 52.22% vs 51.16%), particularly benefiting from RGB-TIR fusion in adverse conditions
Reproducibility commitment: Plans to release benchmark data, framework codes, model implementations, and evaluation toolkits to enable community adoption and future research

High-quality presentation: Well-organized paper with informative visualizations, comprehensive 30-page appendix containing detailed per-scene/weather/illumination results, qualitative comparisons, and ablations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in baseline method: AMA is essentially asymmetric LoRA (straightforward adaptation of existing technique), and LAVS uses standard cross-attention—the true contribution is the benchmark, not algorithmic innovation; no comparison to alternative modality adaptation strategies

Annotation quality verification gaps: Proportion of manually verified instances not specified, no inter-annotator agreement metrics (Cohen's kappa, Fleiss' kappa) provided, and LVLM annotation dependency creates potential for systematic biases not fully explored

Data selection bias: Selecting largest instance per image may bias toward salient objects; long-tail category filtering reduces diversity; imbalanced scene distribution (Urban 13K vs Waterfront 807 instances) not thoroughly discussed

Insufficient modality complementarity analysis: Limited mechanistic understanding of when/why RGB+TIR helps; missing attention visualizations showing modality contributions; marginal improvements in well-lit conditions lack significance analysis; no exploration of failure modes where fusion hurts performance

Experimental limitations: Missing result indicators ('-' entries in Tables 4-5 unexplained), train/test splits follow source dataset boundaries rather than random partitioning (potential systematic bias), only Acc@0.5 metric used (Acc@0.7 would strengthen claims), zero-shot evaluation de-emphasized as expected yet still heavily presented

Insufficient AMA design justification: Limited theoretical or empirical justification for asymmetric rank selection (rv ≤ rt); no ablation comparing to symmetric LoRA or exploring rank sensitivity; hierarchical design mentioned but not detailed or ablated separately

Application-specific scope limitations: Benchmark heavily weighted toward outdoor urban/rural scenes from vehicle detection datasets; limited indoor scenarios; generalization to other domains unexplored; results may not transfer to alternative RGB-TIR collection modalities or sensor types

Missing critical analyses: No cross-dataset transfer evaluation (train on RefFLIR → test on RefM3FD); no backward compatibility assessment on existing RGB-only benchmarks; limited exploration of TIR failure modes (reflective surfaces, thermal homogeneity); insufficient justification for why LAVS outperforms simpler fusion strategies

strengths: First comprehensive RGB-Thermal visual grounding benchmark addressing a genuine gap in existing RGB-only benchmarks; well-motivated by practical challenges of low illumination and adverse weather

High-quality, large-scale dataset with 40K+ images and multi-level fine-grained annotations (13 scene types, 4 weather conditions, 4 illumination levels, object properties); significantly more challenging than existing benchmarks (43.2% weak-light vs. 0.9-10.7% in RefCOCO)
Rigorous annotation pipeline with clear filtering criteria, multi-stage verification (15% manual review, 5% editing, 0.5% removal), and statistical validation of annotation consistency

Comprehensive experimental evaluation of 11 representative models across three modalities with extensive fine-grained analysis on scenes, weather, illumination, object size, and occlusion; clear, actionable insights (scene complexity sensitivity, LoRA robustness, low-light failures, MLLM limitations)
Reproducible baseline (RGBT-VGNet) with well-motivated components and proper ablation studies; clear documentation enables reproduction
Planned public release of dataset, code, checkpoints, and evaluation scripts without hidden test sets strengthens community value
Excellent presentation with clear motivation, comprehensive tables, and extensive supplementary material including full annotation protocols
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty in RGBT-VGNet: AMA is straightforward asymmetric LoRA allocation; LAVS applies standard text-guided cross-attention; TPF uses simple heuristics with fixed equal weighting rather than learned parameters. While positioned as 'reference baseline,' technical contribution remains incremental

RGB-TIR spatial alignment not quantitatively analyzed: paper mentions 'spatially aligned or weakly aligned pairs' but provides no metrics on alignment error or filtering statistics, making benchmark quality assessment incomplete

Mixed MLLM evaluation results undermine practical promise: Tables 8-9 show MLLMs often degrade with RGB+TIR input (Qwen3.5-Plus: 50.52%→47.62% on RefFLIR-test at 224×224); explanation lacks depth; some models produce no output; results highly resolution-dependent. Suggests technology may not be deployment-ready despite benchmark's existence

Dataset composition concerns: only 3 source datasets with RefMFAD comprising 55.5% of total data; no cross-dataset generalization analysis; missing study of scene/weather distribution across sources; potential representation bias not addressed

Difficulty distribution imbalance: TestA achieves 91%+ for top methods (relatively easy) with large gap to TestB/TestC (49-64%), suggesting unbalanced evaluation spectrum; no analysis of condition balance across train/val/test splits

Insufficient statistical rigor: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or inter-annotator agreement metrics; variance across training runs not reported; only percentage statistics provided for quality control

Limited thermal-specific analysis: no dedicated study of when thermal helps/hurts; TIR-specific failure modes not discussed; temperature variations across seasons/locations not considered; characteristics distinguishing TIR from RGB underexplored

Hyperparameter choices lack justification: LoRA rank allocation (rv=16, rt=48) chosen empirically (Table 10) without principled justification; fixed equal weighting in TPF without ablation; no comparison of learned vs. heuristic fusion strategies
API-based MLLM evaluation not reproducible: GLM-4.6V, Kimi-K2.5, Qwen3.5-Plus version-dependent with no open-source baselines; results may not replicate as models evolve
Missing generalization validation: no evaluation on external RGBT datasets; no cross-dataset generalization analysis; no sim-to-real or dataset bias assessment
